title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
author: Anonymous
era: Mesopotamia, second to first millennium BCE, with roots in earlier Sumerian poems
openingChapterLabel: Tablet I — Gilgamesh rules Uruk, and Enkidu is made
openingText: Let the man who tested everything to its depths teach his people. Let him who knows it all instruct them all. Let him give them his wisdom to share. [Gilgamesh?] knew all things. He found the hidden secret […] and handed down the account from before the flood. He travelled far. Worn out by the journey, he carved all his labours on a stone tablet. He built the high walls of Uruk. He fastened the foundations of holy Eanna, where the treasure lay, firm as bronze. He strengthened its base so no one could pass […] the threshold which from ancient times […].
about: Gilgamesh rules Uruk and gives its people no peace. When they complain to the gods, Aruru shapes a man out of clay. Enkidu has never eaten bread or set foot in a city. He brings Gilgamesh to a halt the only way he knows how: he stands in the doorway. What begins as a wrestling match becomes a friendship. When Gilgamesh loses his friend, no victory can give him peace.

angleCards.title: What does a king do with his power?
angleCards.text: When Uruk complains, the gods decide someone must be able to stand up to Gilgamesh. Notice who still dares to challenge him once he has a friend.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow who can stand up to the king and whether he learns to listen.

angleCards.title: Losing a friend
angleCards.text: Gilgamesh feels for Enkidu's heartbeat. Later he tells almost everyone he meets about his friend. What can he say now that he could never say while Enkidu lived?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to listen to the way Gilgamesh speaks to Enkidu and about him.

angleCards.title: What does a repetition reveal?
angleCards.text: The hunter describes the wild man to his father, then to the king. The same words come back, but the stakes change the next time they are spoken.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to notice who takes up someone else's words and why.

angleCards.title: Where does the story break off?
angleCards.text: A change of tablet can send you back to a scene you've just read. Brief notes mark breaks in the text and places where a different witness takes over.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to tell a repetition inside the poem from a change of textual witness.

cast.name: Gilgamesh
cast.description: He is two thirds divine and one third human. At first no one can stop him. Later he cannot stop the very thing he most fears.

cast.name: Enkidu
cast.description: Aruru shapes him from clay on the steppe. He runs with the animals before learning to live among people.

cast.name: Ninsun
cast.description: Gilgamesh brings her his dreams. When he proposes to fight Humbaba she climbs onto the roof to ask the sun god for help.

cast.name: Ishtar
cast.description: She wants to marry Gilgamesh. When he lists what has happened to her past lovers she takes her grievance to her father Anu.

cast.name: Siduri
cast.description: She bars her door at the sight of Gilgamesh. In an older version she advises him to take pleasure in the life he already has.

cast.name: Utnapishtim
cast.description: He tells Gilgamesh how he built a ship and what happened when the gods discovered that someone had survived.

whyItMatters.title: A city in place of an answer
whyItMatters.body: Gilgamesh travels to the edge of the world to ask how he can avoid dying. At the end of the eleventh tablet he asks someone to look closely at the bricks of his own city.

whyItMatters.title: Who tells the story of the water?
whyItMatters.body: Utnapishtim remembers the light on his cheek when he opened the hatch after the flood. An entire city's destruction is told by one man who sat weeping in a boat.

whyItMatters.title: About this reading text
whyItMatters.body: This text follows R. Campbell Thompson's English edition of 1928. It brings together witnesses from different periods and languages. […] marks a break, [?] an uncertain reading. The twelfth tablet is a separate story about the underworld. Later discoveries and readings can give a different sequence.
